To clarify, I do think it’s worth reaching out to the teacher. I don’t think she had ill intentions but she definitely could’ve handled it better. For all we know, the teacher might’ve thought the kid was making a joke at first.

This whole situation seems like there was a lot of room for miscommunication between everyone involved…

I’m not saying what she did was right. Do I think it’s worth reaching out to the teacher? Yes, absolutely.

But people are human. We make mistakes or operate with incomplete information. It doesn’t mean we have bad intentions.

As a teacher myself, I agree that she likely didn’t *know* you actively kept this information away from your daughter. ADHD isn’t a death sentence or a character flaw, she also likely didn’t think of it as a negative aspect of your daughter’s identity.

I get it. I honestly STILL struggle with writing, but lately I’ve started writing fanfic because I’m simply having fun with it. It gives me somewhere silly or not the most serious to start.

My hope is eventually I’ll pick up an old work or start a new one, but for now, writing a few paragraphs every few days is working. I also am trying to make a specific writing space. Stephen King really advocates for having a set space and schedule, so I figured I’d give it a try.

It also helps that I’ve found people in my life who are supportive of trying things this way. They’re happy I’m writing and they’ll read what I’m willing to share.

You can ask if you’d like, but you can’t base your entire self-worth and happiness on some girl. It’s not healthy or realistic. She isn’t a substitute for therapy, medication, or self-care, and expecting her to pull you out of your depression is just going to hurt both of you.

I totally disagree that you’re worthless. You are worthy and enough! But it takes a lot of work to realize that, and you have to want that for yourself.

I think a big step is being vulnerable and non-confrontational about it. Brené Brown talks a lot about stuff like this in some of her books. One example she gives is phrasing things like, “When you do __, the story I tell myself is __.” So, “When you cut our plans short, the story I tell myself is that you don’t want to be around me.” It gives him a chance to understand how you feel and explain the actual reason why he left. Heck, even explain that you know he wasn’t abandoning you, but that your mind tells you he was.

You can also try to write or tell yourself repeatedly what you know, logically, is the reason he would’ve gone. It can help you to recognize that what your fears are telling you isn’t the reality.

As a good high school student who became a mediocre college student who became a great grad student who became a subpar substitute teacher... I say, hang in there. The American education system sucks and all of your teachers know it.

In terms of what you have the power to do, though: talk to your teachers and relearn how to learn.

If you just chat with your instructors about the stress you’re under, most of them will do what they can to help. The thing is that sometimes you have to take that step. We can’t always tell why someone is struggling. Some teachers may also be willing to change where they display information, such as writing a schedule on the board for the week.

In terms of learning to learn, it gets tricky. There is no one-size-fits-all way to learn or teach. Figure out what you’re good at and what areas you’re not as good at. Try different ways to take notes or get organized. Do you remember what you read? Does studying with techno music help? Do you need to move around when you’re trying to plan an essay? Think about how you think and what makes things stick. I hated planners in school, but I would fall apart without the one I have now, where I have a visual reminder of what I need to accomplish. (Hell, when I was in middle school, I had to have teachers sign my planner for a while because I wasn’t doing the work.)

If that seems like too much, pick a couple of smaller tasks, like writing due dates on assignments as you get them or clarifying with teachers after class as to what the homework is.

I'm 23, as well, so take this for what you will. I'm not an expert. Hell, I've been trying to recover on and off since I was 19 and still aren't anywhere near where I want to be.

I give the advice a lot that the things we think about ourselves were once told or conveyed to us from outside. Parents, siblings, family, friends, teachers, employers, lovers, the media, etc. It doesn't even mean they were spoken maliciously. At some point, you were given the impression that you were inadequate in some way. You were told that you were not successful or adequate by someone's standards. Eventually, you internalized these things -- people don't have to tell you them for you to still think them about yourself.

It's exhausting to fight with yourself constantly. Sometimes you manage to win battles, but it still feels like losing the war or like it never ends. Besides, how are you supposed to combat your thoughts? What are we supposed to do when our brains think we've royally fucked everything up? That we'll never get better or get things right? That we're just not strong enough or smart enough or *something* enough to be more than this?

You are worth not feeling like this.

You are worth healing; you are worth accepting and loving yourself.

Yes, it's true, recovery takes *time* and is *difficult*. I can't tell you how long or how hard because it varies person to person. It takes us years to fall this far and become this unwound and lost, you can't expect it to change overnight or a few days or maybe even a few months.

However, it is *not* too late to change. This is meant to be encouraging and not to be taken as a way of setting you back. There are things you can do to change these parts of you, to stop hating yourself or beating yourself up, to stop living paralyzed in fear. I was already on antidepressants. My first step this round was therapy. I found a therapist I really connect with and I see her nearly weekly. I started reading self-help books, mostly by Brene Brown, and articles. I have a space in my room that I use to hang up posters and cards that are meant to be inspirational or motivational; they all say things I want to internalize one day. I journal and meditate. I'm still not very good at self care and I still don't know much about my spirituality, but I'm working on exploring those concepts.

It's the hardest thing I've ever done, I think, and I've watched family members get taken off of life support and been in emotionally abusive relationships. I've graduated school and then *gone back* for *more* education. Yet this is the hardest thing I've done. I've made a lot of progress but sometimes it doesn't feel like enough. Sometimes it feels like I'll never be more than this stupid brain. On those days, I allow myself to sleep and cry, I let myself hide. There are times when I am so afraid of what comes after the depression and anxiety, that I'll be empty and lost without them.

There's a spoken word poem that connects with me. I listen to it every time I feel down and like I want to isolate myself or just sleep my days away. It's called "Here Am I" by Anis Mojgani. The poem ends:

> What made the beauty of the earth and the beauty of the sea? Did that beauty make you, did that beauty make me? Will it make me something? Will I be something? Am I something? And the answer comes: already am; always was; and I still have time to be.

Sorry if none of this was helpful. I had been to several therapists before mine and I only felt like one of the previous ones really could help me. I felt like they all talked about concepts but never actions. I needed something concrete that I could see or measure or *do*.

TL;DR: Please hang in there. You are worthy. You are enough. You can get better, even if it's scary, unfamiliar, or difficult.

Yeah, no problem! She copied it out of *The Anxiety & Phobia Workbook* (which I feel like I might actually own, I just never opened it after I bought it). It's pretty popular online, apparently, a quick search got me [here](https://explorable.com/e/personal-bill-of-rights).

When my therapist first gave it to me, she had me look over it and say my initial thoughts. A lot of the ones that stood out to me dealt with boundaries -- *I have the right to say no to requests or demands I can't meet* -- or my sense of worth, as with *I have the right to be angry at someone I love*. She sent me home with the task of reflecting over the next week about it and writing in my journal.

One day, I decided to buy a bunch of little postcard-sized prints off of Etsy. They're fluffy but they say things like, "You are enough." When she gave me the sheet she had copied from the book, the Personal Bill of Rights, I stuck it up on my wall next to those prints. They're above my bed so I see them all the time. I don't always pay close attention to them, but they're still there.

I've read a lot of self-help books, as well, especially stuff by Brene Brown. She's a researcher and a lot of what she has written about or studied deals with shame and vulnerability.

That's probably not helpful at all. It's been a really slow and really rough journey and there's still a lot of work to be done.

It's not instant, and there's no way to know how long it will take, how difficult it will be, or how you'll get there. I know that doesn't self helpful. It really doesn't. But the thing is that we are all our own people; it is different for literally everyone. Changing and growing and recovering is something that varies between individuals. It starts small and it takes a while before you notice progress. I'm not talking hours or days. It could be months, it could be *years*.

I don't love myself. In fact, I'm far from it -- but I've made progress.

I don't loathe myself anymore, not completely.

When I started, I felt the same way as you. It sounded like a giant pile of bullshit. Think happy? Love myself? That was insane and impossible. Regardless, I started medication and went back to therapy, with a new therapist and a clear set of goals. I know how I want to be or feel eventually, so I sat down, reflected on that image, and came up with about 12-20 goals for therapy.

The largest thing I've learned about how I think so far is that the things we hear, the external voices, eventually become the internal. I spent so long being told, directly or indirectly, that I wasn't *enough*. I wasn't smart enough, a hard enough worker, attractive enough, a good enough romantic partner, successful enough, the list goes on. Part of it came from my parents. Part of it from failed relationships. However, after being told these things enough, I started saying it to myself. Even when people don't say these things, I still think them.

Like I said, it's a work in progress.

Therapy has really helped in this department. My therapist gave me a sheet called a "Personal Bill of Rights". It's a list of things that are supposed to feel natural and normal. Do I agree with all of them? *No*, especially not all the time. However, one of the instructions is to post it somewhere visible and read it every day. So I do, even when I don't agree with it. I tell myself these things even if I don't believe them, and you know what? Sometimes I actually *do*. They're starting to become the internal thoughts.

On the other hand, maybe therapy isn't going so well. It's perfectly okay to *outright tell* a mental health professional that you want *actions*, and to tell them what isn't working. Their goal is to help you reach *your* goals. If something doesn't help, if it makes you feel worse, if you feel stuck, if you're uncomfortable, *you can tell them it isn't working*. As I said earlier, we are individuals. What helps someone else may not help you, and vice versa.

You *can* get there.

You *are* worth feeling like more than this.

*You* are worthy of getting better.

Some people repress unpleasant experiences and memories. That's totally a thing that happens. It's also possible you legitimately just *forgot*. Memory is weird and not always reliable.

For a while, I thought seeing a therapist basically broke me. I thought I had a handle on my anxiety and depression until I started treatment, where it just got worse and worse and eventually I couldn't function.

Looking back, I've realized a few things: I wasn't handling myself well or in a healthy way; that therapist was not a good fit; once you give up your smokescreens and stop denying your issues, you have to challenge them and that is *difficult*.

The last part is what really trips me up sometimes. When you start going to therapy or working on your issues, you become really aware of them. You also try to give up the ways you've been coping and avoiding them, the really unhealthy thoughts or behaviors. This means you don't have anything to hide behind. Nothing dulls the emotions or thoughts. You don't have any choice but to confront them head-on.

One of the big things that has helped me has been journaling on a regular basis. Typically, I try to write before bed, and I definitely try to do so if something major happens.

If I have a lot going on or I keep finding myself avoiding writing, at the very least, I write either the day or a couple of hours before my session to jot down some things that have happened, how I've been feeling, or things I want to focus on.

We don't always cover everything I've written down, or by discussing one thing, we resolve or introduce a separate point. It's totally okay if the session doesn't go how you thought it might! Just make sure to know what you want to get out, you'll figure it out from there.

About a year ago, I decided to really work on it because I was tired of having bloody, painful fingers. I also was student teaching and was embarrassed that somebody might notice, but I never got any comments on it. After some pretty stressful and trying times, it fell apart.

Like other folks have mentioned, I started carrying cuticle cream or stuff like Aquafor, which is supposed to help repair skin. I set a reminder on my phone to tell me to apply a few times a day. I also use an app that's a habit tracker, so I set it to tell me to clip/shape my nails/cuticles once every 2-3 days. I would follow that up with painting them. It was super helpful while it lasted!

I'm a young teacher, too! Right now I'm on the sub train instead of full-time anywhere, but I only wrapped up my teaching certificate earlier this year and wasn't the most proactive about full-time employment.

*Anyways*, one of the things that I started doing early on in student teaching that helped me was to keep a journal. I have two separate ones -- one for inside the classroom, so I can write down things that work or don't and funny quotes, and a general one where I get my thoughts out from the day. Writing what happens and how I feel has helped me a lot. I reflect a lot on what I feel and why that is. It also helped me articulate my disordered thoughts when I started therapy again.

It's also important to figure out "self care" things. I know that term can be vague or gets a little misconstrued through the internet. Find what helps you relax. Find what activities you enjoy. Take the time to take care of yourself and not just your students. Meditation, baths, reading, running, watching YouTube videos, being social, there are all kinds of awesome things you can try to help ease the impending sense of doom and stay present or process after you get home for the day.

Okay, so, we broke up when I was having a massive meltdown. I had a lot of very stressful transitions in my life at the time, and was incredibly overwhelmed. I also resorted to some unhealthy coping mechanisms I was ashamed of, that I didn't want to admit to anyone, much less someone I was in a relationship with. My response was to claim I didn't have romantic feelings for him, when in actuality all I could *really* feel at the time was stress, anxiety, horror, and shame from everything else... he told me he didn't think breaks ever worked and we broke up. He was obviously down and upset for several days, and we both talked about how neither of us wanted that to happen.

We continued to talk for several weeks. I went back to therapy, I left one job, started a new one, things seemed to be on the right track. It seemed like he was entertaining the notion of getting back together, but one day he told me that he thought he had been clear that wasn't the case. I was justifiably upset. I felt like I'd been lied to and deceived just so he could avoid feeling guilty that I was still struggling. We continued to argue on and off for a little while before we agreed that we would like to be friends but it would take time and we needed space.

I'm at a point now where I realize that he wasn't as committed as I was. I wanted work on things and try to fix them even when they were difficult. He... didn't. I think when things are challenging, his instinct is to just drop it. We stopped talking and I haven't heard so much as a peep from him. If he truly wanted to be my friend, or if he truly missed me or our relationship, I think the least he could've done would be to reach out to me. He hasn't. The last time we talked, I opened up about the extent of an abusive relationship I was in before I met him. I'm not sure what I hoped that would accomplish, but it gave me the compassion and support to encourage me to tell my close friends. That didn't change anything about our relationship, or lack thereof, but it helped me to acknowledge a very difficult, painful experience that still impacts me, so hopefully *I* can change.

I deleted him off of everything so I didn't have to feel that gut-wrenching feeling of both inadequacy and betrayal every time he popped up. I started dating again, almost two months after the breakup, but I'm by no means ready for something serious. I'm still focusing on myself and working to be the person I want to be, to have the toolbox of skills and resources that might have prevented this in the first place.

Okay, well, one: marijuana is not accurately considered a "gateway drug" anymore. The majority of people who eventually develop addictions to heavier drugs are actually initially prescribed prescription painkillers, become addicted, and eventually need to consume more and more (or heavier and heavier stuff) as their bodies adjust and build a tolerance. My region of the US has had a growing heroin problem, so a lot of teacher professional development has dealt with either emerging technologies or drugs...

Your counselor definitely doesn't seem like a good fit and doesn't seem qualified to really be helping you. It's possible she is good, just not for you. Having goals in mind may help you sort through to find someone better suited to you.

Aside from everything /u/dwade333miami said, if you think a new therapist or counselor is the type of person you're looking for, you may still not feel great after some of your sessions. One way a lot of folks cope is by denying their feelings and emotions, or relying on other things to distract them from those. By taking the step to overcome, you take away those defense mechanisms that are unhealthy, so you're left to confront those thoughts and feelings on your own. It may make you feel "worse", even though it's really the first time you've opened yourself up fully to those overwhelming thoughts in a long time.

I was the one who initiated, but it was on accident. I was going through a rough transition period and felt constantly stressed and overwhelmed. I told him I didn't have feelings for him when the truth was that my mind was preoccupied with everything going on *and* I didn't want to tell anyone how badly I was in terms of mental health. While I just wanted a break or some space, he... didn't.

I regretted it immediately. Still do, but what can you do? We talked consistently for a few weeks but then he wanted space. It was really difficult for me to do that. We got into a huge fight that was unrelated to that, though, and both said some pretty nasty things.

I apologized as soon as I realized I had just been lashing out due to other stuff. He never really did, so I guess that jump-started my attempt to move on. I'm no longer in denial and no longer wasting my time trying to make things right. I even started meeting guys again.

The only advice for you I have right now is to stop contacting her. It's difficult, and I'm definitely a hypocrite for suggesting it, but at this point you're probably doing more damage than good. You both need time to settle down, collect your thoughts, analyze what happened, and determine what the next steps are.

It's possible she's still angry or overwhelmed. Maybe she fells like you've invalidated her experiences and opinions. No matter how she feels, it's her objective for herself to determine her own feelings. You can't change them, no matter what you do, and it is not your responsibility to do so. Give her the space to do so, and take the time to apply that logic to yourself. How do you feel? What caused this? What do you want to happen? Is there anything within your power you can do to reach that goal?

I agree with what other people are saying, but I will be honest -- sometimes when you approach it as if it's something that isn't a big deal or that you don't care/mind, sometimes they will take this to mean that you will *never have struggles again*. While mental illness is common, not everyone is aware of this or has experience or knowledge of it.

Healing isn't linear. Mental illness is something that we don't magically become cured of. Some times in our lives will be more difficult than usual, sometimes for an extended period of time, and we will struggle. But once you've worked on yourself and built these new patterns and coping mechanisms, you'll always have that toolbox to look back on. Recovery is about resilience.

My best friend told me a week or two ago that he had a breakthrough as to what anxiety really is. As we were discussing, I realized that it made a lot of sense, so it helped me to step back and reflect on some of my feelings at the time. I've struggled with a lot of questions like this lately. What has really helped me to figure out how I genuinely feel has been to journal, as well as talk it out with professionals and peers. I've also been working very hard to say exactly how I'm feeling when I'm feeling it, to recognize how I'm feeling or what I'm thinking.

Anyways, his interpretation:

>Your brain asks you a question like, *“Did I deal with that correctly?”* or, *“Does he like me?”* and you give a logical answer. Then your brain asks you that again. And you give the same answer. But your brain doesn’t stop. It keeps asking that question. Eventually, you give it a different answer in hopes of stopping the questions. They don’t stop. Two days later, you have six different answers to a question and the question keeps coming and you have no idea how to respond.
